lines.cap: **Narrator:** Wednesday. The school hall. Mr Hargreaves is on mug number fifteen.
**Mr H:** Practice run. One **unseen poem**. Prep with a pen, then a **three-to-five-minute spoken analysis**.
**Timer:** Coach Timer! Ten minutes prep on the clock! Move those eyeballs, people!
**Mei:** Sir, I've never seen this poem before! What if I guess the wrong secret meaning?!
**Mike:** Please don't panic into me. I'm Mike. I have terrible stage fright, and 'um' gives me hives.
**Mei:** Testing... **Um, this poem is basically about**... lots of techniques?
**Mike:** SQUEEEEAK! She said 'um'! AND 'basically'! AND 'lots of techniques'!
**Nib:** My ink! Right onto the stage floor! Technique-listing is not an argument, darling!
**Will:** In my Globe, groundlings pelted actors with turnips for less! Stand tall, child!
**Mei:** Unseen poetry: **one star**. Even the microphone is sweating.
**Narrator:** All the School's a Stage. Episode ten: Unseen, Unheard Of.
**Narrator:** Period 4. Room 8H. Mr Hargreaves confiscates Mei's highlighter.
**Mr H:** First: there is **no single secret meaning**. An unseen tests your **method**, not your memory.
**Timer:** Read it **more than once**! Read One: the **literal story**. Read Two: **shifts and structure**. Read Three: **language and sound**!
**Mr H:** On your first read, ask **WHAT** is happening with **TSST**: **Title, Speaker, Situation, Tone**.
**Nib:** Say '**the speaker**' or '**persona**', never assume it's the poet! Christina Rossetti is not literally ghost-writing from the grave.
**Mei:** Let's try Edward Thomas's **Adlestrop**. Gist: a train stops at a quiet country station, and a blackbird sings.
**Mei:** Wait — what does '**Unwontedly**' mean?! My whole talk is ruined!
**Mr H:** Use context. An express train stopping at a tiny empty village? It means **unusually**. One hard word never sinks you.
**Nib:** Next read: **HOW** does it work? Annotate **feature plus effect** — never write 'sibilance' without 'so what?'
**Mr H:** Don't list ten devices. Pick **two or three rich details** and **zoom in** on single words for **connotations**.
**Will:** Take '**cage**': literally bars, yet it connotes **imprisonment**, being **owned**, being **on display** — or even **protection**!
**Mei:** Or in 'The sky **unzips** at four o'clock' — 'unzips' sounds sudden and cheeky, like Singapore rain flinging open a bag!
**Mike:** Three moments explored deeply... instead of ten yelled at me? Oh, my grille feels calmer already.
**Narrator:** Thursday. The library. Will is pointing dramatically at line nine of everything.
**Mr H:** Almost every poem **changes**. Spot that shift and your talk has a spine: **before, turn, after**.
**Will:** In a sonnet, the turn is the **volta**! Watch Christina Rossetti's Petrarchan sonnet, **Remember**.
**Nib:** Lines one to eight, the **octave**, repeat the plea: 'Remember me when I am gone away.'
**Mei:** Then line nine starts with '**Yet**'! 'Yet if you should forget me for a while...'
**Will:** And the **sestet** releases them: 'Better by far you should **forget and smile** / Than that you should remember and be sad.'
**Mr H:** Look for **turn words** — *but, yet, still, now, however* — or shifts in **tense**, **tone**, or **place**.
**Mei:** Like W. B. Yeats's **The Lake Isle of Innisfree**! Two stanzas of dreamy island peace, 'bee-loud glade'...
**Nib:** Then stanza three shifts to the city: 'While I stand on the roadway, or on the **pavements grey**.' Innisfree is only in his '**deep heart's core**'!
**Mr H:** Always check the **title**, **opening** and **ending**. Adlestrop opens 'Yes.' — like answering a friend mid-conversation.
**Kevin:** And in 'The steam hissed. Someone cleared his throat.' — full-stop **caesura**! Two tiny sounds in huge silence! That's me!
**Mei:** Then 'only the name' **enjambs** across the stanza break into wild flowers and birds! Two stars — no, three!
**Narrator:** Lunchtime. Coach Timer is drilling Mei's ten-minute prep routine.
**Timer:** Split your prep! Ten percent **gist**, forty percent **annotate**, thirty-five percent **cue card**, fifteen percent **whispered rehearsal**!
**Mr H:** Your first thirty seconds need a **thesis**: an arguable big idea that every point proves.
**Mei:** Like: 'Paul Laurence Dunbar's **Sympathy** is about a bird in a cage that wants to get out'?
**Nib:** That merely **retells**, darling! Use the formula: '**On the surface... but really...**'
**Will:** Listen to Dunbar: 'It is not a carol of joy or glee, / But a **prayer** that he sends from his heart's deep core.'
**Mei:** **On the surface**, Sympathy describes a trapped bird, **but really** its prayer-like song explores human suffering and the ache for freedom!
**Mr H:** Now structure your four-minute talk: **Only Lazy Students Forget Proper Conclusions**.
**Timer:** **Overview** thesis! **Language** point! **Structure** point! **Form** point! **Personal response**! **Conclusion** returning to your thesis!
**Mei:** I'll write out all five hundred and fifty words and read them super fast!
**Mike:** NO! Reading a full script makes you stare at your shoes in a flat robot voice! Use a **cue card**!
**Mr H:** Three columns on one small card: **Point**, **short Quote**, **Effect word**. Glance down, then talk to us.
**Narrator:** Thursday afternoon. Mei steps back up to Mike on the hall stage.
**Mike:** Remember **PEEP** up from your notes: **Pace, Eye contact, Emphasis, and Pauses**! Swap 'um' for a calm silent pause!
**Mr H:** Guide the listener with **signposting**: 'My first point focuses on...', 'Moving on to structure...', 'To conclude...'
**Nib:** And use **tentative phrasing**: 'This **could suggest**', '**perhaps**'. It shows poems hold multiple meanings.
**Mei:** So: 'It could maybe perhaps possibly suggest the bird might sort of be sad'?
**Mr H:** One hedge is thoughtful; five is soup. Be tentative about interpretation, **confident** with evidence.
**Will:** Never say 'quote, unquote'! Slow down slightly and lift your voice so we **hear** the quotation marks!
**Mei:** Watch me climb the ladder on Adlestrop! **Point**: Moving to structure, the final stanza shifts from silence to vast song.
**Mei:** **Evidence**: One blackbird sings, then '**Farther and farther**, all the birds / Of Oxfordshire and Gloucestershire.'
**Mei:** **Explain**: Repeating 'farther' and rolling out those long county names makes the birdsong **ripple outwards**.
**Mei:** **Link**: **Evaluating** this alongside 1914 context, perhaps that ordinary minute feels like a last glimpse of peaceful England.
**Mike:** Not one 'um'! Eye contact! Embedded quote! I didn't squeak once!
**Timer:** Four minutes on the dot! Now: **teacher follow-up questions**!
**Mr H:** Mei. You argued Dunbar's Sympathy is about pain. Could someone argue the ending is actually **hopeful**?
**Kevin:** He challenged her! Abort! Breathe into the bag! Say 'I don't know' and run!
**Mr H:** A follow-up question isn't a trap — it's a chance to lift your mark by **thinking on your feet**.
**Timer:** Use **PACE**: **Pause**, **Answer directly**, **Cite the poem**, **Extend or Evaluate**!
**Mei:** That's an interesting question — let me look at the last stanza again.
**Mei:** I can see a hopeful reading, because the bird flings a '**plea, that upward to Heaven**' reaches — he hasn't given up.
**Mei:** **However**, his wing is still '**bruised**' and the cage never opens, so I think the hope is real, yet painful and fragile.
**Nib:** Magnificent! Five mark-scheme pillars: **Understanding, Analysis, Terminology, Personal response, and Delivery**.
**Will:** And for **personal response**, never just say 'I liked it'! Name a line that lingered — like Dickinson's '**It asked a crumb - of me.**'
**Mr H:** You paused, went back to the text, and weighed two readings. Top marks.
**Narrator:** Before the next speaker enters the hall, the cast would like to save you some marks.
**Mei:** Memory hooks! **TSST** on Read One; **Only Lazy Students Forget Proper Conclusions** to structure your talk.
**Mike:** **PEEP** up from your cue card for delivery, and **PACE** for follow-up questions!
**Mr H:** One. Don't **retell** the poem stanza by stanza. Open with an '**On the surface... but really...**' thesis.
**Nib:** Two. Never **feature-spot** ten techniques. Explore **three rich moments** with connotations and effects.
**Mike:** Three. Don't read a **full script** to your shoes! Speak from keyword notes and swap 'um' for silence.
**Will:** Four. Don't confuse the **speaker** with the **poet**, and never ignore the **volta** or the ending!
**Kevin:** Five. Keep quotations **short and embedded** — voice them by slowing down, never 'quote unquote'!
**Timer:** Six. At a follow-up question, never say 'I don't know' and stop — **pause** and check the poem!
**Mei:** Unseen spoken analysis: **four and a half stars**! Mike didn't faint, and I sounded like an actual critic.
**Will:** Where is the other half-star?!
**Mei:** Ten minutes prep is stressful, lah.
**Mr H:** Quick-fire quiz! Say each answer out loud before it appears.
**Mr H:** What does **TSST** stand for on your first read of an unseen poem?
**Mei:** **Title, Speaker, Situation, and Tone**.
**Mr H:** What is the Italian term for the **turning point** or shift in a poem?
**Will:** The **volta**! Look for turn words like 'yet' or 'but'.
**Mr H:** Complete the thesis formula: '**On the surface** the poem describes..., **but**...'
**Nib:** '...**but really** it explores...' — moving from literal gist to deeper meaning.
**Mr H:** Should you bring a **word-for-word script** or a **brief cue card** to a spoken analysis?
**Mike:** A **brief cue card** of keywords and short quotes — so you look up and talk!
**Mr H:** What four steps help you handle a follow-up question: **PACE**?
**Timer:** **Pause, Answer directly, Cite the poem, and Extend or Evaluate**!
**Mr H:** Brilliant work. Now try the **Unseen Poems & Spoken Analysis** quiz in your English Lab.
**Will:** Mike! Ready for my four-hour Hamlet soliloquy?!
**Mike:** Unplugging myself now. Goodbye.
